vocal_caveat: IMPORTANT: The vocal emotion channel is the second weakest of the four, after facial emotion, and is explicitly down-weighted. Benchmarked on 150 hand-rated clips from 6 speakers (vocal_bench/), the adopted model scores 48.9% three-class accuracy on held-out speakers - better than the model it replaced, which at 34.0% was significantly worse than always guessing NEUTRAL (p = 0.0070), but still not reliably better than that constant. No model tested beat it. Conflicts attributed to the vocal channel alone are damped accordingly, and per-segment claims should not rest on this channel. Read the within-video figure, not the headline: this report compares segments inside one video, and the channel's rank correlation with human judgement measured within a video is +0.159 across 147 clips and +0.056 on unseen speakers (vocal_bench/SPEAKER_NORM_RESULT.md). Most of its apparent accuracy is a between-video effect that says more about the speaker's habitual energy than about any individual moment.

all_segments.text: Inside this package is the brand new iPhone 18 Pro,
iPhone 18 Pro Max, as well as every key accessory.
And I have spent the last week deep diving into these devices. The changes that seem boring,
but have actually made a huge difference. The changes that seem huge, that have actually made almost zero difference.
And the surprising way that new can be worse.
So I managed to get the 18 Pro in two terabyte in this burgundy color that everyone seems to be after.
The phone's on top. There's the braided USB-C cable plus SIM ejector,
and then Apple's little free book. It's not a page turner.
And then for the 18 Pro Max, I got the black.
And I'm surprised to say I actually prefer it. This is the blackest that a Pro has ever been.
And it's also two terabyte. Which makes what I'm holding in my hands,
the most expensive iPhone ever, until the Duo comes out at a staggering $2,500.
And then to top it all off, the entire Burgundy care package.
All the official cases and straps that Apple's selling. But to be honest, compared to the vibrancy
of that orange that they made last year, Burgundy feels a little too sensible for my liking.
More importantly though, the single boldest claim that Apple made on stage is that the iPhone 18 Pro Max
has not just the largest battery ever on an iPhone,
but also the largest increase in battery ever on an iPhone.
So where do the new phones actually end up versus other iPhones?
And also the competition with Samsung's S26 Ultra.
So I used a combination of apps that I'd say are medium
to high intensity, timed how long it took for them to die,
and blummin' heck, I was not quite ready for this one.
As expected, the base iPhone 17 and 17 Pro were the first to dip
at under nine hours. Samsung's S26 Ultra was a fair margin ahead
at 10 hours on the dot. But then what I've never seen before
is the smaller 18 Pro almost entirely matching the 17 Pro Max,
which hit 10 hours 36. And more impressively, the 18 Pro Max?
Different ball game. Different ball game. In fact, different stadium, to be honest,
with 12 hours and 32. So we're off to a very good start here.
Biggest jump indeed. And now they're drained. What about charging?
So I connected each phone up to its respective ideal wall charger,
because the iPhones and Samsung's use slightly different charging protocols.
And exactly 20... No, okay, not quite one second.
20 minutes later, that was pretty good. We've got 58% and 63% for the latest iPhones.
So it's good to see that they are solidly ahead of the 45% and 50% that last gen got.
Notice also how the smaller Pros charge faster than the bigger ones, because of their not as large batteries.
The base iPhone 17 is somewhere in the middle, but not a single iPhone surpasses Samsung's S26 Ultra.
Apple's kind of caught up, but they're not exactly leading the charge, as it were.
And there's actually an even more important thing that we can use these chargers to test.
Thermals. This is where things start to get a little bit odd, because this is an iPhone 16 Pro Max.
It doesn't have a vapor chamber at all. This is the 17 Pro Max.
It has a vapor chamber, but kind of looks like a strip going down the middle.
The vapor chamber on the 18 Pro and Pro Max, though, occupies almost the entire breadth of the phone.
So to find out how much of a difference it makes, I started a 4K video recording on each,
while plugging them all in for an hour. This is about the most heat
that any normal person is gonna be generating. And here's what happened, recorded on our new state-of-the-art thermal camera.
The whiter the area, the hotter it is. The iPhone 16 Pro Max and the Samsung sort of trade blows as the hottest.
But what I didn't expect to see is that the iPhone 18 Pro Max performed almost identically to the 17 Pro Max.
And that the further the tests went on, if anything, the hotter the body of the 18 Pro Max got.
To the point where, by the end, it was the hottest. So I decided to run the exact same test again the next day, just to be sure,
and we got the exact same result. Well, that's weird. There weren't a lot of new things announced for these 18 Pros,
but one of the only major ones was this three times larger vapor chamber.
So you'd expect the 18 Pro to stay cold as a cucumber, right?
Well, I've just done another test that goes a long way towards explaining why this is happening.
I thought, well, if there's any other way to see if the cooling's doing anything,
it's going to show up in performance. So I decided to put each device through 3DMark's extreme stress test.
20 minutes of them in a continuous loop of 4K graphics rendering.
This is the phone's worst nightmare. I did this multiple times, and these were the best results that each phone achieved.
And yes, the 18 with its new A20 Pro chip absolutely murdered the other devices.
Look at this top score, 9024, which compares to Samsung in second place with 7970,
the iPhone 17 Pro at 5911, and then the 16 Pro with 4860.
And the 18 Pro Max retains this very significant lead,
even if you look at its lowest score during the tests. 6,153.
That handily beats out all the others. But look at the thermals.
The more the test goes on, just like we noticed when we were using the cameras,
if anything, the 18 Pro Max is getting the hottest out of all the phones.
Why? Well, turns out this is actually the vapor chamber doing its job.
What it's not doing, clearly, is stopping the phone itself,
the screen that you see here, the sides and the back, from heating up.
But what it is doing, as you can tell by how this phone is able to
maintain its incredibly high performance numbers, is getting heat away from the chip.
So the outsides of the phone are getting warmer, because it's redistributing the heat from its core more efficiently.
Whereas on some phones, particularly the 16 Pro Max, which doesn't look very hot at all from the front,
the heat isn't escaping, it's trapped inside. And this would also explain why, every single time I got the phones all hot and bothered,
and then removed that strain, the 18 Pro Max is the fastest phone to cool down.
However, if the gaming performance of the A20 Pro is the thing that I expected to be a little,
but has ended up a lot, the AI side of things is kind of the opposite.
Apple promised us two times the AI performance of the 17 Pro,
and while running Geekbench's AI test, I can see a decent 30% or so increase.
First of all, that's not 2x, and secondly, I wasn't able to feel even that performance gain in
any day-to-day task. Like, let's make a Genmoji. Surprised but happy dinosaur, who is riding a skateboard and looks like they're just about to
fall over. Also, they're wearing an astronaut helmet.
Okay, so why isn't the 18 Pro Max not by far the quickest?
What about photo cleanup? I imported one of my favourite group shots, and tried to remove the most handsome
person from the image, because it just wasn't fair.
Why does the 16 Pro Max actually finish first? And it's not like there's any difference in quality,
the outputs look the same. I tried again using the fast cleanup option, which is strictly always on
device. The 18 did win this one, but then asking Siri to make me a shortcut, one of the main newly
introduced iOS features. 18 Pro came squarely in last place. Now, there do seem to be some
third-party apps where you can see clear benefits to the new chip. Like when I used Grid AI to generate
a highly detailed high-resolution image. This was about 1.8 times faster on 18 Pro versus 17 Pro,
and 2.5 times faster on 17 versus 16. But it's just a shame that, at least right now,
this theoretical performance is not translating to the real-life experience that most people are going to
care about on their phones. Now, before one of the big letdowns, one completely random thing that I
thought was cool is, you know the dynamic island has gotten smaller on the 18 Pros, right? Well,
it's pretty interesting how. So from the last phone, they've taken the infrared camera from Face ID,
the thing that fires out the dots onto your face to figure out your 3D contours, and they've put that
behind the screen and in the top left. But then, to make sure that the IR can still travel through it,
they've had to create gaps. So if you look over here, you can see that they've halved the number of
pixels for the entire area in front of the camera. And then, to try and make sure that you can't tell,
they've rearranged those pixels into a new structure, they've increased each one's brightness to make up
for the fact that there's fewer of them, and also created this smooth gradient between the normal
pixel arrangement and this alternative region. So there's no seam that looks jarring. It's very cool,
the thought that goes into it, and Face ID still works absolutely fine. The only annoying thing is that
when the screen is off and you're looking from a certain angle, you can see it, and it annoys me.
That said, if you were to ask Apple, what's the one flagship feature of these 18 Pros,
Apple would tell you its variable aperture. But while what it's doing is very impressive,
what you're generally getting? Not so much.
So as a general rule, when you're taking photos on a smartphone, the wider your aperture, the better.
Because, well, let's take two shots on this 18 Pro. The first with the aperture set to its widest,
f1.4. Second with the aperture set to narrowest, f4.0. Which of these looks better to you?
It's the wide, right? Because a wide aperture creates so much more depth and character.
Now the one key exception to this is when you're shooting multiple subjects at different depths.
Because let's say one of your subjects is closer to the camera than the other, then maybe you don't
want one subject in focus and the other one blurred out. So one thing that I gotta say the iPhone
18 Pro does do rather intelligently is adapt this aperture to your situation. So notice it's pretty
wide at f1.8. The whole time it's just me. It stays at f1.8 when someone else enters, because it knows
